S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter — S1.1.1 (SL)
Understanding: Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. Compounds consist of atoms of different elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Mixtures contain more than one element or compound in no fixed ratio, which are not chemically bonded and so can be separated by physical methods.
Skills: Distinguish between the properties of elements, compounds and mixtures.
Guidance: Solvation, filtration, recrystallization, evaporation, distillation and paper chromatography should be covered. The differences between homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures should be understood.
Linking questions: Tool 1—What factors are considered in choosing a method to separate the components of a mixture? | Tool 1—How can the products of a reaction be purified? | Structure 2.2—How do intermolecular forces influence the type of mixture that forms between two substances? | Structure 2.3—Why are alloys generally considered to be mixtures, even though they often contain metallic bonding?

S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter — S1.1.2 (SL)
Understanding: The kinetic molecular theory is a model to explain physical properties of matter (solids, liquids and gases) and changes of state.
Skills: Distinguish the different states of matter. Use state symbols (s,, g and aq) in chemical equations.
Guidance: Names of the changes of state should be covered: melting, freezing, vaporization (evaporation and boiling), condensation, sublimation and deposition.
Linking questions: Structure 2.4—Why are some substances solid while others are fluid under standard conditions? | Structure 2 (all), Reactivity 1.2—Why are some changes of state endothermic and some exothermic?

S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter — S1.1.3 (SL)
Understanding: The temperature, T, in Kelvin (K) is a measure of average kinetic energy E k of particles.
Skills: Interpret observable changes in physical properties and temperature during changes of state. Convert between values in the Celsius and Kelvin scales.
Guidance: The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of temperature and has the same incremental value as the Celsius degree (°C).
Linking questions: Reactivity 2.2—What is the graphical distribution of kinetic energy values of particles in a sample at a fixed temperature? | Reactivity 2.2—What must happen to particles for a chemical reaction to occur?

S1.2 The nuclear atom — S1.2.1 (SL)
Understanding: Atoms contain a positively charged, dense nucleus composed of protons and neutrons (nucleons). Negatively charged electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus.
Guidance: A Use the nuclear symbol Z X to deduce the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms and ions. Relative masses and charges of the subatomic particles should be known; actual values are given in chemical properties of atoms? the data booklet. The mass of the electron can be considered negligible.
Linking questions: Structure 1.3—What determines the different | Structure 3.1—How does the atomic number relate to the position of an element in the periodic table?

S1.2 The nuclear atom — S1.2.2 (SL)
Understanding: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
Skills: Perform calculations involving non-integer relative atomic masses and abundance of isotopes from given data.
Guidance: Differences in the physical properties of isotopes should be understood. Specific examples of isotopes need not be learned.
Linking questions: Nature of science, Reactivity 3.4—How can isotope tracers provide evidence for a reaction mechanism?

S1.2 The nuclear atom — S1.2.3 (AHL)
Understanding: Mass spectra are used to determine the relative atomic masses of elements from their isotopic composition.
Skills: Interpret mass spectra in terms of identity and relative abundance of isotopes.
Guidance: The operational details of the mass spectrometer will not be assessed.
Linking questions: Structure 3.2—How does the fragmentation pattern of a compound in the mass spectrometer help in the determination of its structure?

S1.3 Electron configurations — S1.3.1 (SL)
Understanding: Emission spectra are produced by atoms emitting photons when electrons in excited states return to lower energy levels.
Guidance: Qualitatively describe the relationship between colour, wavelength, frequency and energy across the electromagnetic spectrum. Distinguish between a continuous and a line spectrum. Details of the electromagnetic spectrum are given in the data booklet.

S1.3 Electron configurations — S1.3.2 (SL)
Understanding: The line emission spectrum of hydrogen provides evidence for the existence of electrons in discrete energy levels, which converge at higher energies.
Skills: Describe the emission spectrum of the hydrogen atom, including the relationships between the lines and energy transitions to the first, second and third energy levels.
Guidance: The names of the different series in the hydrogen emission spectrum will not be assessed.
Linking questions: Inquiry 2—In the study of emission spectra from gaseous elements and of light, what qualitative and quantitative data can be collected from instruments such as gas discharge tubes and prisms? | Nature of science, Structure 1.2—How do emission spectra provide evidence for the existence of different elements?

S1.3 Electron configurations — S1.3.3 (SL)
Understanding: The main energy level is given an integer number, n, and can hold a maximum of 2 n 2 electrons.
Skills: Deduce the maximum number of electrons that can occupy each energy level.
Linking questions: Structure 3.1—How does an element’s highest main energy level relate to its period number in the periodic table?

S1.3 Electron configurations — S1.3.4 (SL)
Understanding: A more detailed model of the atom describes the division of the main energy level into s, p, d and f sublevels of successively higher energies.
Skills: Recognize the shape and orientation of an s atomic orbital and the three p atomic orbitals.
Linking questions: Structure 3.1—What is the relationship between energy sublevels and the block nature of the periodic table?

S1.3 Electron configurations — S1.3.5 (SL)
Understanding: Each orbital has a defined energy state for a given electron configuration and chemical environment, and can hold two electrons of opposite spin. Sublevels contain a fixed number of orbitals, regions of space where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
Skills: Apply the Aufbau principle, Hund’s rule and the Pauli exclusion principle to deduce electron configurations for atoms and ions up to Z.
Guidance: =36 Full electron configurations and condensed electron configurations using the noble gas core should be covered. Orbital diagrams, i.e. arrow-in-box diagrams, should be used to represent the filling and relative energy of orbitals. The electron configurations of Cr and Cu as exceptions should be covered.

S1.3 Electron configurations — S1.3.6 (AHL)
Understanding: In an emission spectrum, the limit of convergence at higher frequency corresponds to ionization.
Skills: Explain the trends and discontinuities in first ionization energy (IE) across a period and down a group. Calculate the value of the first IE from spectral data that gives the wavelength or frequency of the convergence limit.
Guidance: The value of the Planck constant h and the equations E = hf and c = λf are given in the data booklet.
Linking questions: Structure 3.1—How does the trend in IE values across a period and down a group explain the trends in properties of metals and non-metals? | Nature of science, Tool 3, Reactivity 3.1—Why are log scales useful when discussing [H+] and IEs?

S1.3 Electron configurations — S1.3.7 (AHL)
Understanding: Successive ionization energy (IE) data for an element give information about its electron configuration.
Skills: Deduce the group of an element from its successive ionization data.
Guidance: Databases are useful for compiling graphs of trends in IEs.
Linking questions: AHL Structure 3.1—How do patterns of successive IEs of transition elements help to explain the variable oxidation states of these elements?

S1.4 Counting particles by mass: The mole — S1.4.1 (SL)
Understanding: The mole (mol) is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly the number of elementary entities given by the Avogadro constant.
Skills: Convert the amount of substance, n, to the number of specified elementary entities.
Guidance: An elementary entity may be an atom, a molecule, an ion, an electron, any other particle or a specified group of particles. The Avogadro constant N A is given in the data booklet. It has the units mol–1.

S1.4 Counting particles by mass: The mole — S1.4.2 (SL)
Understanding: Masses of atoms are compared on a scale relative to 12C and are expressed as relative atomic mass A r and relative formula mass M r.
Skills: Determine relative formula masses M r from relative atomic masses A r.
Guidance: Relative atomic mass and relative formula mass have Structure 3.1—Atoms increase in mass as their no units. The values of relative atomic masses given to two decimal places in the data booklet should be used in calculations.
Linking questions: position descends in the periodic table. What properties might be related to this trend?

S1.4 Counting particles by mass: The mole — S1.4.3 (SL)
Understanding: Molar mass M has the units g mol–1.
Skills: Solve problems involving the relationships between the number of particles, the amount of substance in moles and the mass in grams. m
Guidance: The relationship n = is given in the data booklet. M
Linking questions: Reactivity 2.1—How can molar masses be used with chemical equations to determine the masses of the products of a reaction?

S1.4 Counting particles by mass: The mole — S1.4.4 (SL)
Understanding: The empirical formula of a compound gives the simplest ratio of atoms of each element present in that compound. The molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element present in a molecule.
Guidance: Interconvert the percentage composition by mass and the empirical formula. Determine the molecular formula of a compound from its empirical formula and molar mass.
Linking questions: Tool 1—How can experimental data on mass changes in combustion reactions be used to derive empirical formulas? | Nature of science, Tool 3, Structure 3.2—What is the importance of approximation in the determination of an empirical formula?

S1.4 Counting particles by mass: The mole — S1.4.5 (SL)
Understanding: The molar concentration is determined by the amount of solute and the volume of solution.
Skills: Solve problems involving the molar concentration, amount of solute and volume of solution.
Guidance: The use of square brackets to represent molar concentration is required. Units of concentration should include g dm–3 and mol dm–3 and conversion between these. The relationship n = CV is given in the data booklet.
Linking questions: Tool 1—What are the considerations in the choice of glassware used in preparing a standard solution and a serial dilution? | Tool 1, Inquiry 2—How can a calibration curve be used to determine the concentration of a solution?

S1.4 Counting particles by mass: The mole — S1.4.6 (SL)
Understanding: Avogadro’s law states that equal volumes of all gases measured under the same conditions of temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
Skills: Solve problems involving the mole ratio of reactants and/or products and the volume of gases.
Linking questions: Structure 1.5—Avogadro’s law applies to ideal gases. Under what conditions might the behaviour of a real gas deviate most from an ideal gas?

S1.5 Ideal gases — S1.5.1 (SL)
Understanding: An ideal gas consists of moving particles with negligible volume and no intermolecular forces. All collisions between particles are considered elastic.
Skills: Recognize the key assumptions in the ideal gas model.

S1.5 Ideal gases — S1.5.2 (SL)
Understanding: Real gases deviate from the ideal gas model, particularly at low temperature and high pressure.
Skills: Explain the limitations of the ideal gas model.
Guidance: No mathematical coverage is required.
Linking questions: Structure 2.2—Under comparable conditions, why do some gases deviate more from ideal behaviour than others?

S1.5 Ideal gases — S1.5.3 (SL)
Understanding: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
Guidance: Investigate the relationship between temperature, pressure and volume for a fixed mass of an ideal gas and analyse graphs relating these variables. The names of specific gas laws will not be assessed. The value for the molar volume of an ideal gas under accurately plotted data points. What are the standard temperature and pressure (STP) is given in the data booklet.
Linking questions: Nature of science, Tools 2 and 3, Reactivity 2.2— Graphs can be presented as sketches or as advantages and limitations of each representation?

S1.5 Ideal gases — S1.5.4 (SL)
Understanding: The relationship between the pressure, volume, temperature and amount of an ideal gas is shown in the ideal gas equation PV = nRT
Skills: Solve problems relating to the ideal gas equation.
Guidance: Units of volume and pressure should be SI only. The value of the gas constant R, the ideal gas equation, and the combined gas law, are given in the data booklet.
Linking questions: P V P V and the combined gas law 1 1 2 2. T = T 1 2 | Tool 1, Inquiry 2—How can the ideal gas law be used to calculate the molar mass of a gas from experimental data?

S2.1 The ionic model — S2.1.1 (SL)
Understanding: When metal atoms lose electrons, they form positive ions called cations. When non-metal atoms gain electrons, they form negative ions called anions.
Skills: Predict the charge of an ion from the electron configuration of the atom.
Guidance: The formation of ions with different charges from a transition element should be included.
Linking questions: Structure 3.1—How does the position of an element in the periodic table relate to the charge of its ion(s)? AHL Structure 1.3—How does the trend in successive ionization energies of transition elements explain their variable oxidation states?

S2.1 The ionic model — S2.1.2 (SL)
Understanding: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
Skills: Deduce the formula and name of an ionic compound from its component ions, including polyatomic ions.
Guidance: Binary ionic compounds are named with the cation first, followed by the anion. The anion adopts the suffix “ide”. Interconvert names and formulas of binary ionic compounds. The following polyatomic ions should be known by name and formula: ammonium NH+, 4 hydroxide OH–, compound from its elements a redox reaction? nitrate NO –, hydrogencarbonate HCO –, carbonate 3 3 CO2–, sulfate SO2–, phosphate PO3–. 3 4 4
Linking questions: Reactivity 3.2—Why is the formation of an ionic AHL Structure 2.2—How is formal charge used to predict the preferred structure of sulfate? AHL Reactivity 3.1—Polyatomic anions are conjugate bases of common acids. What is the relationship between their stability and the conjugate acid’s dissociation constant, K a ?

S2.1 The ionic model — S2.1.3 (SL)
Understanding: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
Skills: Explain the physical properties of ionic compounds to include volatility, electrical conductivity and solubility.
Guidance: Include lattice enthalpy as a measure of the strength Tool 1, Inquiry 2—What experimental data of the ionic bond in different compounds, influenced by ion radius and charge.
Linking questions: demonstrate the physical properties of ionic compounds? | Structure 3.1—How can lattice enthalpies and the bonding continuum explain the trend in melting points of metal chlorides across period 3?

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.1 (SL)
Understanding: A covalent bond is formed by the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei. The octet rule refers to the tendency of atoms to gain a valence shell with a total of 8 electrons.
Skills: Deduce the Lewis formula of molecules and ions for up to four electron pairs on each atom.
Guidance: Lewis formulas (also known as electron dot or Lewis structures) show all the valence electrons (bonding and non-bonding pairs) in a covalently bonded species. Electron pairs in a Lewis formula can be shown as dots, crosses or dashes. Molecules containing atoms with fewer than an octet of electrons should be covered. Organic and inorganic examples should be used.
Linking questions: Nature of science—What are some of the limitations of the octet rule? | Structure 1.3—Why do noble gases form covalent bonds less readily than other elements? | Structure 2.1—Why do ionic bonds only form between different elements while covalent bonds can form between atoms of the same element?

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.2 (SL)
Understanding: Single, double and triple bonds involve one, two and three shared pairs of electrons respectively.
Skills: Explain the relationship between the number of bonds, bond length and bond strength.
Linking questions: Reactivity 2.2—How does the presence of double and triple bonds in molecules influence their reactivity?

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.3 (SL)
Understanding: A coordination bond is a covalent bond in which both the electrons of the shared pair originate from the same atom.
Skills: Identify coordination bonds in compounds.
Guidance: AHL—Include coverage of transition element complexes.
Linking questions: AHL Reactivity 3.4—Why do Lewis acid–base reactions lead to the formation of coordination bonds?

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.4 (SL)
Understanding: The valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) model enables the shapes of molecules to be predicted from the repulsion of electron domains around a central atom.
Skills: Predict the electron domain geometry and the molecular geometry for species with up to four electron domains.
Guidance: Include predicting how non-bonding pairs and multiple bonds affect bond angles.
Linking questions: Nature of science—How useful is the VSEPR model at predicting molecular geometry?

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.5 (SL)
Understanding: Bond polarity results from the difference in electronegativities of the bonded atoms.
Skills: Deduce the polar nature of a covalent bond from electronegativity values.
Guidance: Bond dipoles can be shown either with partial charges or vectors. Electronegativity values are given in the data booklet.
Linking questions: Structure 2.1—What properties of ionic compounds might be expected in compounds with polar covalent bonding?

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.6 (SL)
Understanding: Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and molecular geometry.
Skills: Deduce the net dipole moment of a molecule or ion by considering bond polarity and molecular geometry.
Guidance: Examples should include species in which bond dipoles do and do not cancel each other.
Linking questions: AHL Structure 3.2—What features of a molecule make it “infrared (IR) active”?

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.7 (SL)
Understanding: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.
Skills: Describe the structures and explain the properties of silicon, silicon dioxide and carbon’s allotropes: diamond, graphite, fullerenes and graphene.
Guidance: Allotropes of the same element have different bonding and structural patterns, and so have different chemical and physical properties.
Linking questions: Structure 3.1—Why are silicon–silicon bonds generally weaker than carbon–carbon bonds?

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.8 (SL)
Understanding: The nature of the force that exists between molecules is determined by the size and polarity of the molecules. Intermolecular forces include London (dispersion), dipole-induced dipole, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding.
Skills: Deduce the types of intermolecular force present from the structural features of covalent molecules.
Guidance: The term “van der Waals forces” should be used as an inclusive term to include dipole–dipole, dipole- induced dipole, and London (dispersion) forces. Hydrogen bonds occur when hydrogen, being covalently bonded to an electronegative atom, has an attractive interaction on a neighbouring electronegative atom.
Linking questions: Structure 1.5—To what extent can intermolecular forces explain the deviation of real gases from ideal behaviour? | Nature of science, Structure 1.1, 2.1, 2.3—How do the terms “bonds” and “forces” compare? | Nature of science—How can advances in technology lead to changes in scientific definitions, e.g. the updated International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) definition of the hydrogen bond?

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.9 (SL)
Understanding: Given comparable molar mass, the relative strengths of intermolecular forces are generally: London (dispersion) forces < dipole–dipole forces < hydrogen bonding.
Skills: Explain the physical properties of covalent substances to include volatility, electrical conductivity and solubility in terms of their structure.
Linking questions: Tool 1, Inquiry 2—What experimental data demonstrate the physical properties of covalent substances? | Structure 3.2—To what extent does a functional group determine the nature of the intermolecular forces?

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.10 (SL)
Understanding: Chromatography is a technique used to separate the components of a mixture based on their relative attractions involving intermolecular forces to mobile and stationary phases.
Guidance: Explain, calculate and interpret the retardation factor values, R F. Knowledge of the use of locating agents in chromatography is not required. The technical and operational details of a gas chromatograph or high-performance liquid chromatograph will not be assessed.
Linking questions: Tool 1—How can a mixture be separated using paper chromatography or thin layer chromatography (TLC)?

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.11 (AHL)
Understanding: Resonance structures occur when there is more than one possible position for a double bond in a molecule.
Skills: Deduce resonance structures of molecules and ions.
Guidance: Include the term “delocalization”.
Linking questions: Structure 1.3—Why are oxygen and ozone dissociated by different wavelengths of light?

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.12 (AHL)
Understanding: Benzene, C 6 H 6, is an important example of a molecule that has resonance.
Skills: Discuss the structure of benzene from physical and chemical evidence.
Linking questions: Reactivity 2.1, 2.2—How does the resonance energy in benzene explain its relative unreactivity? | Reactivity 3.4—What are the structural features of benzene that favour it undergoing electrophilic substitution reactions?

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.13 (AHL)
Understanding: Some atoms can form molecules in which they have an expanded octet of electrons.
Guidance: Visually represent Lewis formulas for species with five and six electron domains around the central atom. Deduce the electron domain geometry and the molecular geometry for these species using the VSEPR model.
Linking questions: Structure 3.1—How does the ability of some atoms to expand their octet relate to their position in the periodic table?

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.14 (AHL)
Understanding: Formal charge values can be calculated for each atom in a species and used to determine which of several possible Lewis formulas is preferred.
Skills: Apply formal charge to determine a preferred Lewis formula from different Lewis formulas for a species.
Linking questions: Structure 3.1, Reactivity 3.2—What are the different assumptions made in the calculation of formal charge and of oxidation states for atoms in a species?

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.15 (AHL)
Understanding: Sigma bonds σ form by the head-on combination of atomic orbitals where the electron density is concentrated along the bond axis. Pi bonds π form by the lateral combination of p-orbitals where the electron density is concentrated on opposite sides of the bond axis.
Skills: Deduce the presence of sigma bonds and pi bonds in molecules and ions.
Guidance: Include both organic and inorganic examples.

S2.2 The covalent model — S2.2.16 (AHL)
Understanding: Hybridization is the concept of mixing atomic orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals for bonding.
Skills: Analyse the hybridization and bond formation in molecules and ions. Identify the relationships between Lewis formulas, electron domains, molecular geometry and type of hybridization. Predict the geometry around an atom from its hybridization, and vice versa.
Guidance: Include both organic and inorganic examples. Only sp, sp2 and sp3 hybridization need to be covered.

S2.3 The metallic model — S2.3.1 (SL)
Understanding: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalized electrons.
Skills: Explain the electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity and malleability of metals. Relate characteristic properties of metals to their uses.
Linking questions: Tool 1, Inquiry 2, Structure 3.1—What experimental data demonstrate the physical properties of metals, and trends in these properties, in the periodic table? | Reactivity 3.2—What trends in reactivity of metals can be predicted from the periodic table?

S2.3 The metallic model — S2.3.2 (SL)
Understanding: The strength of a metallic bond depends on the charge of the ions and the radius of the metal ion.
Skills: Explain trends in melting points of s and p block metals.
Guidance: A simple treatment in terms of charge of cations and Structure 2.4—What are the features of metallic electron density is required.
Linking questions: bonding that make it possible for metals to form alloys?

S2.3 The metallic model — S2.3.3 (AHL)
Understanding: Transition elements have delocalized d-electrons.
Skills: Explain the high melting point and electrical conductivity of transition elements.
Guidance: Chemical properties of transition elements are covered in Reactivity 3.4.
Linking questions: Structure 3.1—Why is the trend in melting points of metals across a period less evident across the d- block?

S2.4 From models to materials — S2.4.1 (SL)
Understanding: Bonding is best described as a continuum between the ionic, covalent and metallic models, and can be represented by a bonding triangle.
Skills: Use bonding models to explain the properties of a material.
Guidance: A triangular bonding diagram is provided in the data booklet.
Linking questions: Structure 3.1—How do the trends in properties of period 3 oxides reflect the trend in their bonding? | Nature of science, Structures 2.1, 2.2—What are the limitations of discrete bonding categories?

S2.4 From models to materials — S2.4.2 (SL)
Understanding: The position of a compound in the bonding triangle is determined by the relative contributions of the three bonding types to the overall bond.
Skills: Determine the position of a compound in the bonding triangle from electronegativity data. Predict the properties of a compound based on its position in the bonding triangle.
Guidance: To illustrate the relationship between bonding type and properties, include example materials of varying reinforced concretes, which are made from ionic percentage bonding character. Only binary compounds need to be considered. Calculations of percentage ionic character are not required. Electronegativity data are given in the data booklet.
Linking questions: Structure 2.1, 2.2, 2.3—Why do composites like and covalently bonded components and steel bars, have unique properties?

S2.4 From models to materials — S2.4.3 (SL)
Understanding: Alloys are mixtures of a metal and other metals or non-metals. They have enhanced properties.
Skills: Explain the properties of alloys in terms of non-directional bonding.
Guidance: Illustrate with common examples such as bronze, brass and stainless steel. Specific examples of alloys do not have to be learned.
Linking questions: Structure 1.1—Why are alloys more correctly described as mixtures rather than as compounds?

S2.4 From models to materials — S2.4.4 (SL)
Understanding: Polymers are large molecules, or macromolecules, made from repeating subunits called monomers.
Skills: Describe the common properties of plastics in terms of their structure.
Guidance: Examples of natural and synthetic polymers should be discussed.
Linking questions: Structure 3.2—What are the structural features of some plastics that make them biodegradable?

S2.4 From models to materials — S2.4.5 (SL)
Understanding: Addition polymers form by the breaking of a double bond in each monomer.
Skills: Represent the repeating unit of an addition polymer from given monomer structures.
Guidance: Examples should include polymerization reactions of alkenes. Structures of monomers do not have to be learned but will be provided or will need to be deduced from the polymer.
Linking questions: Structure 3.2—What functional groups in molecules can enable them to act as monomers for addition reactions? | Reactivity 2.1—Why is the atom economy 100% for an addition polymerization reaction?

S2.4 From models to materials — S2.4.6 (AHL)
Understanding: Condensation polymers form by the reaction between functional groups in each monomer with the release of a small molecule.
Skills: Represent the repeating unit of polyamides and polyesters from given monomer structures.
Guidance: All biological macromolecules form by condensation Structure 3.2—What functional groups in molecules reactions and break down by hydrolysis.
Linking questions: can enable them to act as monomers for condensation reactions?

S3.1 The periodic table: Classification of elements — S3.1.1 (SL)
Understanding: The periodic table consists of periods, groups and blocks.
Skills: Identify the positions of metals, metalloids and non-metals in the periodic table.
Guidance: The four blocks associated with the sublevels s, p, d, f should be recognized. A copy of the periodic table is available in the data booklet.

S3.1 The periodic table: Classification of elements — S3.1.2 (SL)
Understanding: The period number shows the outer energy level that is occupied by electrons. Elements in a group have a common number of valence electrons.
Skills: Deduce the electron configuration of an atom up to Z table and vice versa.
Guidance: Groups are numbered from 1 to 18. The classifications “alkali metals”, “halogens”, “transition elements” and “noble gases” should be known.
Linking questions: from the element’s position in the periodic =36 | Nature of science, Structure 1.2—How has the organization of elements in the periodic table facilitated the discovery of new elements?

S3.1 The periodic table: Classification of elements — S3.1.3 (SL)
Understanding: Periodicity refers to trends in properties of elements across a period and down a group.
Skills: Explain the periodicity of atomic radius, ionic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity.

S3.1 The periodic table: Classification of elements — S3.1.4 (SL)
Understanding: Trends in properties of elements down a group include the increasing metallic character of group 1 elements and decreasing non-metallic character of group 17 elements.
Skills: Describe and explain the reactions of group 1 metals with water, and of group 17 elements with halide ions.
Linking questions: Inquiry 2, Tool 2—Why are simulations often used in exploring the trends in chemical reactivity of group 1 and group 17 elements?

S3.1 The periodic table: Classification of elements — S3.1.5 (SL)
Understanding: Metallic and non-metallic properties show a continuum. This includes the trend from basic metal oxides through amphoteric to acidic non-metal oxides.
Skills: Deduce equations for the reactions with water of the oxides of group 1 and group 2 metals, carbon and sulfur.
Guidance: Include acid rain caused by gaseous non-metal oxides, and ocean acidification caused by increasing explain the differences in the properties of metal CO 2 levels.
Linking questions: Structure 2.1, 2.2—How do differences in bonding and non-metal oxides?

S3.1 The periodic table: Classification of elements — S3.1.6 (SL)
Understanding: The oxidation state is a number assigned to an atom to show the number of electrons transferred in forming a bond. It is the charge that atom would have if the compound were composed of ions.
Skills: Deduce the oxidation states of an atom in an ion or a compound. Explain why the oxidation state of an element is zero.
Guidance: Oxidation states are shown with a + or – sign followed by the Arabic symbol for the number, e.g. +2, –1. Examples should include hydrogen in metal hydrides (–1) and oxygen in peroxides (–1). The terms “oxidation number” and “oxidation state” are often used interchangeably, and either term is acceptable in assessment. Naming conventions for oxyanions use oxidation numbers shown with Roman numerals, but generic names persist and are acceptable. Examples include NO– nitrate, NO– nitrite, SO2– sulfate, SO2– sulfite. 3 2 4 3
Linking questions: Reactivity 3.2—How can oxidation states be used to analyse redox reactions?

S3.1 The periodic table: Classification of elements — S3.1.7 (AHL)
Understanding: Discontinuities occur in the trend of increasing first ionization energy across a period.
Skills: Explain how these discontinuities provide evidence for the existence of energy sublevels.
Guidance: Explanations should be based on the energy of the electron removed, rather than on the “special stability” of filled and half-filled sublevels.

S3.1 The periodic table: Classification of elements — S3.1.8 (AHL)
Understanding: Transition elements have incomplete d-sublevels that give them characteristic properties.
Skills: Recognize properties, including: variable oxidation state, high melting points, magnetic properties, catalytic properties, formation of coloured compounds and formation of complex ions with ligands.
Guidance: Knowledge of different types of magnetism will not be assessed.
Linking questions: Nature of science, Structure 2.3—What are the arguments for and against including scandium as a transition element?

S3.1 The periodic table: Classification of elements — S3.1.9 (AHL)
Understanding: The formation of variable oxidation states in transition elements can be explained by the fact that their successive ionization energies are close in value.
Skills: Deduce the electron configurations of ions of the first-row transition elements.

S3.1 The periodic table: Classification of elements — S3.1.10 (AHL)
Understanding: Transition element complexes are coloured due to the absorption of light when an electron is promoted between the orbitals in the split d-sublevels. The colour absorbed is complementary to the colour observed.
Skills: Apply the colour wheel to deduce the wavelengths and frequencies of light absorbed and/or observed.
Guidance: Students are not expected to know the different splitting patterns and their relation to the coordination number. The colour wheel and the equation c = λf are given in the data booklet.
Linking questions: Reactivity 3.4—What is the nature of the reaction between transition element ions and ligands in forming complex ions? | Tool 1, Inquiry 2—How can colorimetry or spectrophotometry be used to calculate the concentration of a solution of coloured ions?

S3.2 Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds — S3.2.1 (SL)
Understanding: Organic compounds can be represented by different types of formulas. These include empirical, molecular, structural (full and condensed), stereochemical and skeletal.
Skills: Identify different formulas and interconvert molecular, skeletal and structural formulas. Construct 3D models (real or virtual) of organic molecules.
Guidance: Stereochemical formulas are not expected to be drawn, except where specifically indicated.
Linking questions: Structure 2.2—What is unique about carbon that enables it to form more compounds than the sum of all the other elements’ compounds? | Nature of science, Structure 2.2—What are the advantages and disadvantages of different depictions of an organic compound (e.g. structural formula, stereochemical formula, skeletal formula, 3D models)?

S3.2 Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds — S3.2.2 (SL)
Understanding: Functional groups give characteristic physical and chemical properties to a compound. Organic compounds are divided into classes according to the functional groups present in their molecules.
Skills: Identify the following functional groups by name and structure: halogeno, hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl, alkoxy, amino, amido, ester, phenyl.
Guidance: The terms “saturated” and “unsaturated” should be included.
Linking questions: AHL Structure 2.4—What is the nature of the reaction that occurs when two amino acids form a dipeptide? | Nature of science, Reactivity 3.2, 3.4—How can functional group reactivity be used to determine a reaction pathway between compounds, e.g. converting ethene into ethanoic acid?

S3.2 Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds — S3.2.3 (SL)
Understanding: A homologous series is a family of compounds in which successive members differ by a common structural unit, typically CH 2. Each homologous series can be described by a general formula.
Skills: Identify the following homologous series: alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, halogenoalkanes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, ethers, amines, amides and esters.
Linking questions: Nature of science, Tool 2—How useful are 3D models (real or virtual) to visualize the invisible?

S3.2 Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds — S3.2.4 (SL)
Understanding: Successive members of a homologous series show a trend in physical properties.
Skills: Describe and explain the trend in melting and boiling points of members of a homologous series.
Linking questions: Structure 2.2—What is the influence of the carbon chain length, branching and the nature of the functional groups on intermolecular forces?

S3.2 Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds — S3.2.5 (SL)
Understanding: “IUPAC nomenclature” refers to a set of rules used by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry to apply systematic names to organic and inorganic compounds.
Skills: Apply IUPAC nomenclature to saturated or mono-unsaturated compounds that have up to six carbon atoms in the parent chain and contain one type of the following functional groups: halogeno, hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl.
Guidance: Include straight-chain and branched-chain isomers.

S3.2 Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds — S3.2.6 (SL)
Understanding: Structural isomers are molecules that have the same molecular formula but different connectivities.
Skills: Recognize isomers, including branched, straight-chain, position and functional group isomers.
Guidance: Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols, halogenoalkanes and amines should be included.
Linking questions: AHL Structure 2.2—How does the fact that there are only 3 isomers of dibromobenzene support the current model of benzene’s structure?

S3.2 Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds — S3.2.7 (AHL)
Understanding: Stereoisomers have the same constitution (atom identities, connectivities and bond multiplicities) but different spatial arrangements of atoms.
Skills: Describe and explain the features that give rise to cis - trans isomerism; recognize it in non-cyclic alkenes and C3 and C4 cycloalkanes. Draw stereochemical formulas showing the tetrahedral arrangement around a chiral carbon. Describe and explain a chiral carbon atom giving rise to stereoisomers with different optical properties. Recognize a pair of enantiomers as non-superimposable mirror images from 3D modelling (real or virtual).
Guidance: Nomenclature using the E‐Z system will not be assessed. The terms “chiral”, “optical activity”, “enantiomer” and “racemic” mixture should be understood. Knowledge of the different chemical properties of enantiomers can be limited to the fact that they behave differently in chiral environments. Wedge-dash type representations involving tapered bonds should be used for the representation of enantiomers.

S3.2 Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds — S3.2.8 (AHL)
Understanding: Mass spectrometry (MS) of organic compounds can cause fragmentation of molecules.
Skills: Deduce information about the structural features of a compound from specific MS fragmentation patterns.
Guidance: Include reference to the molecular ion. Data on specific MS fragments are provided in the data booklet.

S3.2 Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds — S3.2.9 (AHL)
Understanding: Infrared (IR) spectra can be used to identify the type of bond present in a molecule.
Skills: Interpret the functional group region of an IR spectrum, using a table of characteristic frequencies
Guidance: (wavenumber/cm–1). Include reference to the absorption of IR radiation by greenhouse gases. Data for interpretation of IR spectra are given in the data booklet.
Linking questions: Structure 2.2—What features of a molecule determine whether it is IR active or not? | Reactivity 1.3—What properties of a greenhouse gas determine its “global warming potential”?

S3.2 Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds — S3.2.10 (AHL)
Understanding: Proton nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H NMR) gives information on the different chemical environments of hydrogen atoms in a molecule.
Skills: Interpret 1H NMR spectra to deduce the structures of organic molecules from the number of signals, the chemical shifts, and the relative areas under signals (integration traces).

S3.2 Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds — S3.2.11 (AHL)
Understanding: Individual signals can be split into clusters of peaks.
Skills: Interpret 1H NMR spectra from splitting patterns showing singlets, doublets, triplets and quartets to deduce greater structural detail.
Guidance: Data for interpretation of 1H NMR spectra are given in the data booklet.

S3.2 Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds — S3.2.12 (AHL)
Understanding: Data from different techniques are often combined in structural analysis.
Skills: Interpret a variety of data, including analytical spectra, to determine the structure of a molecule.

Understanding: Chemical reactions involve a transfer of energy between the system and the surroundings, while total energy is conserved.
Skills: Understand the difference between heat and temperature.
Linking questions: Structure 1.1—What is the relationship between temperature and kinetic energy of particles?

R1.1 Measuring enthalpy changes — R1.1.2 (SL)
Understanding: Reactions are described as endothermic or exothermic, depending on the direction of energy transfer between the system and the surroundings.
Skills: Understand the temperature change (decrease or increase) that accompanies endothermic and exothermic reactions, respectively.
Linking questions: Tool 1, Inquiry 2—What observations would you expect to make during an endothermic and an exothermic reaction?

R1.1 Measuring enthalpy changes — R1.1.3 (SL)
Understanding: The relative stability of reactants and products determines whether reactions are endothermic or exothermic.
Skills: Sketch and interpret energy profiles for endothermic and exothermic reactions.
Guidance: Axes for energy profiles should be labelled as reaction coordinate x, potential energy y.
Linking questions: Structure 2.2—Most combustion reactions are exothermic; how does the bonding in N 2 explain the fact that its combustion is endothermic?

R1.2 Energy cycles in reactions — R1.2.1 (SL)
Understanding: Bond-breaking absorbs and bond-forming releases energy.
Skills: Calculate the enthalpy change of a reaction from given average bond enthalpy data.
Guidance: Include explanation of why bond enthalpy data are average values and may differ from those measured experimentally. Average bond enthalpy values are given in the data booklet.

Understanding: Hess’s law states that the enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the pathway between the initial and final states.
Skills: Apply Hess’s law to calculate enthalpy changes in multistep reactions.

R1.2 Energy cycles in reactions — R1.2.5 (AHL)
Understanding: A Born–Haber cycle is an application of Hess’s law, used to show energy changes in the formation of an ionic compound.
Skills: Interpret and determine values from a Born–Haber cycle for compounds composed of univalent and divalent ions.
Guidance: The cycle includes: ionization energies, enthalpy of atomization (using sublimation and/or bond enthalpies), electron affinities, lattice enthalpy, enthalpy of formation. The construction of a complete Born–Haber cycle will not be assessed.

R1.3 Energy from fuels — R1.3.1 (SL)
Understanding: Reactive metals, non-metals and organic compounds undergo combustion reactions when heated in oxygen.
Skills: Deduce equations for reactions of combustion, including hydrocarbons and alcohols.
Linking questions: Reactivity 2.2—Why is high activation energy often considered to be a useful property of a fuel? | Reactivity 3.2—Which species are the oxidizing and reducing agents in a combustion reaction?

R1.3 Energy from fuels — R1.3.2 (SL)
Understanding: Incomplete combustion of organic compounds, especially hydrocarbons, leads to the production of carbon monoxide and carbon.
Skills: Deduce equations for the incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons and alcohols.
Linking questions: Inquiry 2—What might be observed when a fuel such as methane is burned in a limited supply of oxygen? | Reactivity 2.1—How does limiting the supply of oxygen in combustion affect the products and increase health risks?

R1.3 Energy from fuels — R1.3.3 (SL)
Understanding: Fossil fuels include coal, crude oil and natural gas, which have different advantages and disadvantages.
Skills: Evaluate the amount of carbon dioxide added to the atmosphere when different fuels burn. Understand the link between carbon dioxide levels and the greenhouse effect.
Guidance: The tendency for incomplete combustion and energy released per unit mass should be covered.
Linking questions: Structure 3.2—Why do larger hydrocarbons have a greater tendency to undergo incomplete combustion? AHL Structure 3.2—Why is carbon dioxide described as a greenhouse gas? | Nature of science, Reactivity 3.2—What are some of the environmental, economic, ethical and social implications of burning fossil fuels?

R1.3 Energy from fuels — R1.3.4 (SL)
Understanding: Biofuels are produced from the biological fixation of carbon over a short period of time through photosynthesis.
Skills: Understand the difference between renewable and non-renewable energy sources.
Guidance: Consider the advantages and disadvantages of biofuels. The reactants and products of photosynthesis should be known.

R1.3 Energy from fuels — R1.3.5 (SL)
Understanding: A fuel cell can be used to convert chemical energy from a fuel directly to electrical energy.
Skills: Deduce half-equations for the electrode reactions in a fuel cell.
Guidance: Hydrogen and methanol should be covered as fuels for fuel cells. The use of proton exchange membranes will not be assessed.
Linking questions: Reactivity 3.2—What are the main differences between a fuel cell and a primary (voltaic) cell?

R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity — R1.4.1 (AHL)
Understanding: Entropy, S, is a measure of the dispersal or distribution of matter and/or energy in a system. The more ways the energy can be distributed, the higher the entropy. Under the same conditions, the entropy of a gas is greater than that of a liquid, which in turn is greater than that of a solid.
Skills: Predict whether a physical or chemical change will result in an increase or decrease in entropy of a system. Calculate standard entropy changes, Δ S ⦵, from standard entropy values, S ⦵.
Guidance: Standard entropy values are given in the data booklet.
Linking questions: Structure 1.1—Why is the entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K predicted to be zero?

R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity — R1.4.2 (AHL)
Understanding: Change in Gibbs energy, Δ G, relates the energy that can be obtained from a chemical reaction to the change in enthalpy, Δ H, change in entropy, Δ S, and absolute temperature, T.
Skills: Apply the equation Δ G ⦵=Δ H ⦵ −T Δ S ⦵ to calculate unknown values of these terms.
Guidance: Thermodynamic data values are given in the data booklet. Note the units: H kJ mol–1; S J K–1 mol–1; G kJ mol–1. Δ Δ Δ

Understanding: At constant pressure, a change is spontaneous if the change in Gibbs energy, Δ G, is negative.
Skills: Interpret the sign of Δ G calculated from thermodynamic data. Determine the temperature at which a reaction becomes spontaneous.
Guidance: Δ G takes into account the direct entropy change resulting from the transformation of the chemicals and the indirect entropy change of the surroundings resulting from the transfer of heat energy.
Linking questions: Reactivity 3.2—How can electrochemical data also be used to predict the spontaneity of a reaction?

R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change — R2.1.1 (SL)
Understanding: Chemical equations show the ratio of reactants and products in a reaction.
Skills: Deduce chemical equations when reactants and products are specified.
Guidance: Include the use of state symbols in chemical equations.
Linking questions: Reactivity 3.2—When is it useful to use half- equations?

R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change — R2.1.2 (SL)
Understanding: The mole ratio of an equation can be used to determine: • the masses and/or volumes of reactants and products • the concentrations of reactants and products for reactions occurring in solution.
Skills: Calculate reacting masses and/or volumes and concentrations of reactants and products.
Guidance: Avogadro’s law and definitions of molar concentration are covered in Structure 1.4. The values for A r given in the data booklet to two decimal places should be used in calculations.
Linking questions: Structure 1.5—How does the molar volume of a gas vary with changes in temperature and pressure? | Nature of science, Structure 1.4—In what ways does Avogadro’s law help us to describe, but not explain, the behaviour of gases?

R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change — R2.1.3 (SL)
Understanding: The limiting reactant determines the theoretical yield.
Skills: Identify the limiting and excess reactants from given data. Distinguish between the theoretical yield and the experimental yield.
Linking questions: Tool 1, Inquiry 1, 2, 3—What errors may cause the experimental yield to be i) higher and ii) lower than the theoretical yield?

R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change — R2.1.4 (SL)
Understanding: The percentage yield is calculated from the ratio of experimental yield to theoretical yield.
Skills: Solve problems involving reacting quantities, limiting and excess reactants, theoretical, experimental and percentage yields.

R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change — R2.1.5 (SL)
Understanding: The atom economy is a measure of efficiency in green chemistry.
Skills: Calculate the atom economy from the stoichiometry of a reaction.
Guidance: Include discussion of the inverse relationship between atom economy and wastage in industrial processes. The equation for calculation of the atom economy is given in the data booklet.
Linking questions: Structure 2.4, Reactivity 2.2—The atom economy and the percentage yield both give important information about the “efficiency” of a chemical process. What other factors should be considered in this assessment?

R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change — R2.2.1 (SL)
Understanding: The rate of reaction is expressed as the change in concentration of a particular reactant/product per unit time.
Skills: Determine rates of reaction.
Guidance: Calculation of reaction rates from tangents of graphs of concentration, volume or mass against time should be covered.
Linking questions: Tool 1, 3, Inquiry 2—Concentration changes in reactions are not usually measured directly. What methods are used to provide data to determine the rate of reactions? | Tool 1—What experiments measuring reaction rates might use time as i) a dependent variable ii) an independent variable?

R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change — R2.2.2 (SL)
Understanding: Species react as a result of collisions of sufficient energy and proper orientation.
Skills: Explain the relationship between the kinetic energy of the particles and the temperature in kelvin, and the role of collision geometry.
Linking questions: Structure 1.1—What is the relationship between the kinetic molecular theory and collision theory?

R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change — R2.2.3 (SL)
Understanding: Factors that influence the rate of a reaction include pressure, concentration, surface area, temperature and the presence of a catalyst.
Skills: Predict and explain the effects of changing conditions on the rate of a reaction.
Linking questions: Tool 1—What variables must be controlled in studying the effect of a factor on the rate of a reaction? | Nature of science, Tool 3, Inquiry 3—How can graphs provide evidence of systematic and random error?

R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change — R2.2.4 (SL)
Understanding: Activation energy, E a, is the minimum energy that colliding particles need for a successful collision leading to a reaction.
Skills: Construct Maxwell–Boltzmann energy distribution curves to explain the effect of temperature on the probability of successful collisions.

R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change — R2.2.5 (SL)
Understanding: Catalysts increase the rate of reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway with lower E a.
Skills: Sketch and explain energy profiles with and without catalysts for endothermic and exothermic reactions. Construct Maxwell–Boltzmann energy distribution curves to explain the effect of different values for E a on the probability of successful collisions.
Guidance: Biological catalysts are called enzymes. The different mechanisms of homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts will not be assessed.
Linking questions: Reactivity 2.3—What is the relative effect of a catalyst on the rate of the forward and backward reactions? AHL Structure 3.1—What are the features of transition elements that make them useful as catalysts?

R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change — R2.2.6 (AHL)
Understanding: Many reactions occur in a series of elementary steps. The slowest step determines the rate of the reaction.
Skills: Evaluate proposed reaction mechanisms and recognize reaction intermediates. Distinguish between intermediates and transition states, and recognize both in energy profiles of reactions.
Guidance: Include examples where the rate-determining step is not the first step. Proposed reaction mechanisms must be consistent with kinetic and stoichiometric data.
Linking questions: Reactivity 3.4—Which mechanism in the hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes involves an intermediate?

R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change — R2.2.7 (AHL)
Understanding: Energy profiles can be used to show the activation energy and transition state of the rate-determining step in a multistep reaction.
Skills: Construct and interpret energy profiles from kinetic data.

R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change — R2.2.8 (AHL)
Understanding: The molecularity of an elementary step is the number of reacting particles taking part in that step.
Skills: Interpret the terms “unimolecular”, “bimolecular” and “termolecular”.

R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change — R2.2.9 (AHL)
Understanding: Rate equations depend on the mechanism of the reaction and can only be determined experimentally.
Skills: Deduce the rate equation for a reaction from experimental data.

R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change — R2.2.10 (AHL)
Understanding: The order of a reaction with respect to a reactant is the exponent to which the concentration of the reactant is raised in the rate equation. The order with respect to a reactant can describe the number of particles taking part in the rate- determining step. The overall reaction order is the sum of the orders with respect to each reactant.
Guidance: Sketch, identify and analyse graphical representations of zero, first and second order reactions. Concentration–time and rate–concentration graphs should be included. Only integer values for order of reaction will be assessed.
Linking questions: Tool 1, 3, Inquiry 2—What measurements are needed to deduce the order of reaction for a specific reactant? | Nature of science—Why are reaction mechanisms only considered as “possible mechanisms”?

R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change — R2.2.11 (AHL)
Understanding: The rate constant, k, is temperature dependent and its units are determined from the overall order of the reaction.
Skills: Solve problems involving the rate equation, including the units of k.
Linking questions: Reactivity 3.4—What are the rate equations and units of k for the reactions of primary and tertiary halogenoalkanes with aqueous alkali?

R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change — R2.2.12 (AHL)
Understanding: The Arrhenius equation uses the temperature dependence of the rate constant to determine the activation energy.
Skills: Describe the qualitative relationship between temperature and the rate constant. Analyse graphical representations of the Arrhenius equation, including its linear form.
Guidance: The Arrhenius equation and its linear form are given in the data booklet.

R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change — R2.2.13 (AHL)
Understanding: The Arrhenius factor, A, takes into account the frequency of collisions with proper orientations.
Skills: Determine the activation energy and the Arrhenius factor from experimental data.

Understanding: A state of dynamic equilibrium is reached in a closed system when the rates of forward and backward reactions are equal.
Skills: Describe the characteristics of a physical and chemical system at equilibrium.

Understanding: The equilibrium law describes how the equilibrium constant, K, can be determined from the stoichiometry of a reaction.

Understanding: Le Châtelier’s principle enables the prediction of the qualitative effects of changes in concentration, temperature and pressure to a system at equilibrium.
Skills: Apply Le Châtelier’s principle to predict and explain responses to changes of systems at equilibrium.

Understanding: The reaction quotient, Q, is calculated using the equilibrium expression with non- equilibrium concentrations of reactants and products.
Skills: Calculate the reaction quotient Q from the concentrations of reactants and products at a particular time, and determine the direction in which the reaction will proceed to reach equilibrium.
